title: TCP Congestion Control
summary: Defines TCP's four intertwined congestion control algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. It also covers how TCP should start sending after a long idle period and discusses acknowledgment generation. It obsoletes RFC 2001 and was replaced by RFC 5681.

plainLanguage.summary: When too many cars enter a road, traffic jams. These rules tell computers to start sending slowly, speed up carefully and slow down when messages get lost.

questions: what is slow start in tcp
what is fast retransmit and fast recovery
how does tcp congestion avoidance work
what is the tcp initial window
subtitle: The four rules that tell TCP to start slowly, speed up carefully and back off when packets go missing.

tldr.problem: A TCP sender that pushes data into a network of unknown capacity can flood it, so senders need a way to probe for capacity and to slow down when the network is overloaded.
tldr.mechanism: TCP keeps a congestion window (cwnd) and a slow start threshold (ssthresh). It grows the window with slow start and congestion avoidance, and reacts to loss with fast retransmit and fast recovery.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2581 obsoletes RFC 2001 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 5681, so it is no longer the current definition of these algorithms.

facts.label: Initial window
facts.value: At most 2*SMSS bytes and no more than 2 segments

today: RFC 2581 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2001. It has been obsoleted by RFC 5681 and updated by RFC 3390, so readers should use the newer RFC for the current rules.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2581 specifies four TCP congestion control algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. The text says they were devised in two works by Jacobson, and that their use with TCP is standardized in the host requirements RFC (RFC 1122).

It is an update of RFC 2001. Beyond the four algorithms, it says what a TCP connection should do after a relatively long idle period and it clarifies some points about how acknowledgments (ACKs) are generated.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a rulebook for sharing a busy road. This one is written for computers sending data, so they do not cause a traffic jam.

sections.title: Definitions and Window Variables
sections.content:
The RFC defines a handful of terms used throughout. The sender maximum segment size (SMSS) is the largest segment the sender can transmit, and the receiver maximum segment size (RMSS) is the largest one the receiver will accept. Without an MSS option, the receiver value is 536 bytes. Neither counts the TCP/IP headers and options.

Two windows limit sending. The receiver window (rwnd) is the most recently advertised receiver window. The congestion window (cwnd) is a sender-side limit. A TCP MUST NOT send data with a sequence number higher than the highest acknowledged sequence number plus the minimum of cwnd and rwnd.

Other defined terms are the initial window (IW), the loss window (LW), the restart window (RW) and the flight size, which is the amount of data sent but not yet acknowledged.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two speed limits. One is set by the receiver who says how much it can hold, and one is set by the sender who guesses how much the road can take. You obey the smaller one.

sections.title: Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance
sections.content:
A sender MUST use slow start and congestion avoidance to control how much unacknowledged data it injects. A third variable, the slow start threshold (ssthresh), decides which one applies: slow start when cwnd < ssthresh, congestion avoidance when cwnd > ssthresh. When they are equal either may be used.

The initial window IW MUST be less than or equal to 2*SMSS bytes and MUST NOT be more than 2 segments. A larger initial window from an experimental extension is mentioned only as a guideline for people experimenting, and is not allowed by this standard. The initial ssthresh MAY be arbitrarily high.

In slow start, cwnd grows by at most SMSS bytes for each ACK that acknowledges new data. In congestion avoidance it grows by 1 full-sized segment per round-trip time, commonly done with cwnd += SMSS*SMSS/cwnd on each non-duplicate ACK.

When the retransmission timer detects loss, ssthresh MUST be set to no more than max (FlightSize / 2, 2*SMSS), and cwnd MUST be set to no more than the loss window, which is 1 full-sized segment. The sender then uses slow start up to the new ssthresh.

Using cwnd instead of FlightSize in the ssthresh formula is called out as an easy mistake.
sections.plainLanguage: You start by sending just a little, then double up quickly while things go well. Once you get near the point where trouble started, you speed up slowly. If a message vanishes, you cut your speed way down and begin again.

sections.title: Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery
sections.content:
A receiver SHOULD send an immediate duplicate ACK when an out-of-order segment arrives. Duplicate ACKs can come from dropped segments, from network re-ordering or from replication of segments.

The sender SHOULD use fast retransmit: after 3 duplicate ACKs (4 identical ACKs with nothing in between), it retransmits the apparently missing segment without waiting for the retransmission timer. Fast recovery then governs sending of new data until a non-duplicate ACK arrives, because duplicate ACKs show that segments are still leaving the network.

  1. On the third duplicate ACK, set ssthresh to no more than max (FlightSize / 2, 2*SMSS).
  2. Retransmit the lost segment and set cwnd to ssthresh plus 3*SMSS.
  3. For each additional duplicate ACK, increase cwnd by SMSS.
  4. Transmit a segment if the new cwnd and the receiver's window allow.
  5. When an ACK for new data arrives, set cwnd to ssthresh.

The RFC notes that this algorithm is known not to recover very efficiently from multiple losses in a single flight of packets.
sections.plainLanguage: If the receiver keeps saying 'I am still waiting for number 5' three times, you resend number 5 right away instead of waiting for a timer. You only slow down a little, since the other messages are still getting through.

sections.title: Idle Connections, ACKs and Loss Recovery
sections.content:
After a long idle period the ACK clock has drained, so TCP could blast a cwnd-sized burst. A TCP SHOULD therefore set cwnd to no more than the restart window RW before sending if it has not sent data for longer than the retransmission timeout. For this standard RW = IW.

Receivers SHOULD use the delayed ACK algorithm, but an ACK SHOULD be generated for at least every second full-sized segment, and MUST be generated within 500 ms of the first unacknowledged packet. Out-of-order segments SHOULD be acked immediately, and a receiver MUST NOT generate more than one ACK for each incoming segment, except to update the offered window.

Better loss recovery algorithms, such as ones using selective acknowledgments or the NewReno approach (RFC 2582), are not standardized here but are allowed if they follow the principles of the four algorithms. Loss in two successive windows, or loss of a retransmission, counts as two congestion indications, so cwnd and ssthresh MUST be lowered twice.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have been quiet for a while, you do not shout at full volume. You start soft again. Receivers should also answer often enough, at least every second message, so the sender is never left guessing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the algorithms make TCP slow down on timeouts and duplicate ACKs, an attacker can hurt a connection by causing data packets or ACKs to be lost, or by forging excessive duplicate ACKs. Two congestion events in a row will often cut ssthresh to its minimum of 2*SMSS.

The attack can go the other way too. Forging excessive duplicate ACKs or excessive ACKs for new data could make endpoints more aggressive, and the RFC says this could conceivably drive part of the network into congestion collapse.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could shout fake messages to make senders slow to a crawl, or to make them rush and clog the road.

items.label: Third duplicate ACK
items.desc: Set ssthresh to no more than max (FlightSize / 2, 2*SMSS).

items.label: Retransmit
items.desc: Resend the lost segment and set cwnd to ssthresh plus 3*SMSS.

items.label: More duplicate ACKs
items.desc: Increase cwnd by SMSS for each one.

items.label: Send new data
items.desc: Transmit a segment if cwnd and the receiver window allow.

items.label: ACK for new data
items.desc: Set cwnd to ssthresh (deflate the window).
